title: Remove Linked List Elements
summary: Given the starting node of a linked list and an integer value, eliminate all nodes whose value matches the given integer, then return the updated starting node of the list.
statement: Given the starting node of a linked list and an integer value, eliminate all nodes whose value matches the given integer, then return the updated starting node of the list.
constraints: Remove every matching value while preserving the relative order of all survivors.
Return the new ListNode head, or None if no nodes remain. The head itself may need removal.
hints: Deleting a node is easier when you hold a pointer to its predecessor.
A dummy node before the head makes deleting the first node an ordinary case.
While previous.next exists: bypass it if its value matches; otherwise advance previous. Return dummy.next.
After a deletion, stay at the same predecessor so consecutive matches are checked. A recursive alternative cleans the suffix then keeps or drops the current head.
editorial: Put a dummy node before the input head. Maintain the invariant that previous is the last retained node before the unprocessed suffix. Bypass a matching successor without advancing; advance only when keeping that successor. Returning dummy.next handles empty and all-deleted lists. The recursive recurrence cleans head.next, then returns that cleaned suffix when head.val matches, or head otherwise. It needs O(n) stack space; the iterative reference supports the 10,000-node boundary without changing Python’s recursion limit.

tests.explanation: Remove both nodes holding 6, including the tail. The surviving chain is 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5.
Every node matches, including consecutive matches at the head. Return None, displayed as [].
